title: Ang 947–956: Ramkali ki Var M3
tomorrow: why would anyone sing 'all ties are false' at a wedding?

lines: AN OLD SONG, A NEW MEANING.
THE TUNE OF JODHA AND VIRA.
cards: Movie trailers do it all the time: an old song everybody knows, slowed down, with a new meaning poured into it. Ang 947 does it too.

Above the third Guru's ballad in Ramkali sits a note for the singers: sing this to the tune of the ballad of Jodha and Vira of Purbani. Two warriors, tradition says, whose fight the bards sang in village squares.
So picture the crowd. They already know the tune. They lean in for the battle.
What they get is a different fight.

teach.h: A VAR: A BALLAD FOR HEROES.
teach.b: A var is a ballad, the old form for heroes: stanzas called pauris, sung with drive.
In the Granth's vars, saloks, short verses, sit before the pauris, and Ramkali ki Var, by Guru Amar Das, follows that pattern. The tune note is the clue.
The bards' version was about warriors and a fight that ended in blood.
The Guru's version keeps the beat and moves the battlefield inside: the self against ego, the mind wandering off and coming home to the Name. The hero isn't someone on horseback.
It's the gurmukh, the one who turns toward the Guru. So why borrow the tune? The Granth doesn't explain; it simply gives the instruction.
But one reading is easy to see. People already carried that rhythm in their bodies. It stirred them.
The Guru didn't ask them to drop it.

teach.h: A FAMILIAR BEAT, A WAY IN.
teach.b: He gave the same beat a new story to carry, and a familiar sound became a way in. There's a kind of mercy in that. No one has to learn a strange new melody to hear an old truth.
They only have to listen to the words this time. Same drum, different war.

how: Ragis sing the Granth's vars salok by salok and pauri by pauri; above Ramkali ki Var of Guru Amar Das, the heading names the older ballad whose tune it follows.

s: Ramkali ki Var names an older ballad's tune for singing
the heading says to sing it to the tune of Jodha and Vira of Purbani.
the var tells the story of two warrior brothers
only the tune is theirs; the fight in the pauris is inside, the self against ego.
the Granth explains why the tune was chosen
it simply gives the instruction; the reasons are readers' readings.

games.q: your team plays the same pump-up song before every game. a teammate wants to keep the beat but sing new words about playing fair. by the var's tune note, how might you see it?
o: a familiar beat can carry a new meaning; that's what the Guru's ballad does.
a pump-up beat is for fighting; fairness needs a quiet song of its own.
it's fine only if nobody can recognize the original tune anymore.
games.why: Guru Amar Das kept the war ballad's beat and moved the battlefield inside. the tune stayed recognizable; the story changed.

practice: If you can stand, walk slowly for a minute to a steady beat in your head, left, right, like a ballad's pulse. Then sit for the rest of the time and let the beat keep going in the breath, nowhere to march to.
If you'd like, read the tune note at the top of ang 947, or the pauri on ang 948, first.
